q: How many π electrons are delocalised over the ring in one molecule of benzene?
x: Each of the six sp² carbons gives one electron from its unhybridised p orbital to the ring, so 6 π electrons are shared over all six carbons. Answering 3 counts π bonds of a Kekulé structure instead of electrons.

q: Which reagent, used at room temperature, tells cyclohexene apart from benzene?
x: Cyclohexene adds Br₂ and decolourises bromine water at once; benzene's delocalised ring does not add bromine under these conditions. Both compounds take up hydrogen over hot nickel and both burn, so those tests do not separate them, and neither reacts with aqueous NaOH.

q: How many isomers of molecular formula C₈H₁₀ contain a benzene ring?
x: Ethylbenzene, C₆H₅CH₂CH₃, plus three dimethylbenzenes (1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-). Answering 3 counts only the dimethylbenzenes and forgets ethylbenzene.

q: The carbon–carbon bond order in benzene is:
x: Six π electrons (three π bonds' worth) are shared equally over six C–C bonds, so each bond is a σ bond plus half a π bond: order 1.5. Orders 1 or 2 describe the separate bonds of a single Kekulé structure.

q: Which statement about the two Kekulé structures of benzene is correct?
o: The real molecule is a single resonance hybrid, and neither Kekulé structure exists on its own
The molecule switches rapidly back and forth between the two structures
Half of all benzene molecules have one structure and half have the other
The two structures differ in the positions of the carbon atoms
x: Resonance structures differ only in where the electrons are drawn; the atoms stay put. Benzene is one hybrid with all bonds equal; 'rapid switching' is the common misreading of the resonance arrow ↔ as an equilibrium ⇌.

q: How many structural isomers are there of trichlorobenzene, C₆H₃Cl₃?
x: The possible positions are 1,2,3-, 1,2,4- and 1,3,5-. Other numberings such as 1,2,5- or 1,3,4- are the same compounds as 1,2,4- numbered differently; counting them separately gives too many.

q: Hydrogenation of cyclohexa-1,3-diene to cyclohexane releases 232 kJ mol⁻¹, and hydrogenation of benzene to cyclohexane releases 208 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for C₆H₆ + H₂ → cyclohexa-1,3-diene?
x: By Hess's law, ΔH(benzene → diene) = ΔH(benzene → cyclohexane) − ΔH(diene → cyclohexane) = −208 − (−232) = +24 kJ mol⁻¹. Adding the first H₂ is uphill because it destroys the aromatic ring's stability; subtracting the other way round gives −24.

q: Which reagents convert benzene into chlorobenzene?
o: Cl₂ in bright sunlight with no catalyst
Cl₂ with anhydrous FeCl₃, in the dark
x: FeCl₃ polarises Cl₂ to give the electrophile for substitution: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ → C₆H₅Cl + HCl. In sunlight without a catalyst chlorine adds by free radicals instead, giving C₆H₆Cl₆.

q: When benzene is alkylated with chloromethane and anhydrous AlCl₃, products with two or more methyl groups also form. The reason is that:
o: The methyl group deactivates the ring, so the reaction cannot stop
AlCl₃ adds to the ring and is replaced by methyl groups
Chloromethane decomposes to give methyl free radicals
The methyl group on the product activates the ring, so methylbenzene reacts faster than benzene
x: An alkyl group donates electron density to the ring, so the first product is more reactive than the starting benzene and is alkylated again (polyalkylation). A deactivating group would do the opposite and slow further substitution.

q: Benzenesulphonic acid, C₆H₅SO₃H, is heated with steam in dilute acid. The organic product is:
x: Sulphonation is reversible: C₆H₅SO₃H + H₂O → C₆H₆ + H₂SO₄ when water is in excess and the mixture is hot. Phenol needs fusion of the sulphonate with NaOH, a different reaction.

q: In Friedel–Crafts reactions the aluminium chloride must be anhydrous because:
o: Water reacts with benzene to form phenol
Only anhydrous AlCl₃ can act as an oxidising agent towards benzene
Water reacts with AlCl₃, so it can no longer act as a Lewis acid to form the electrophile
Water changes the product from substitution to addition
x: AlCl₃ works by accepting a lone pair from the halogen of R–Cl or RCO–Cl. Water hydrolyses it (and also gives up a lone pair to it), so no carbocation or acylium ion forms. Benzene does not react with water.

q: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride, CH₃COCl, in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The electrophile that attacks the ring is:
x: AlCl₃ removes Cl⁻ from CH₃COCl: CH₃COCl + AlCl₃ → CH₃CO⁺ + AlCl₄⁻. The acylium ion attacks the ring. AlCl₄⁻ is a by-product and is negative, so it cannot be an electrophile; CH₃⁺ would need chloromethane.

q: In the bromination of benzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃, what happens to the FeBr₃ by the end of the reaction?
o: It is used up, forming FeBr₂
It is regenerated when FeBr₄⁻ takes up the H⁺ lost by the ring, so it acts as a catalyst
It ends up bonded to the benzene ring
It is reduced to iron metal
x: FeBr₃ + Br₂ → Br⁺ + FeBr₄⁻; after Br⁺ attacks, the arenium ion loses H⁺, and H⁺ + FeBr₄⁻ → HBr + FeBr₃. Because it comes back unchanged, only a small amount is needed.

q: 15.6 g of benzene is converted completely into bromobenzene with Br₂ and FeBr₃. All the HBr formed is absorbed in water. What volume of 0.50 mol dm⁻³ NaOH neutralises it? (C₆H₆ = 78 g mol⁻¹)
x: 15.6/78 = 0.20 mol benzene; C₆H₆ + Br₂ → C₆H₅Br + HBr gives 0.20 mol HBr, which needs 0.20 mol NaOH: 0.20/0.50 = 0.40 dm³ = 400 cm³. Multiplying by 0.50 instead of dividing gives 100 cm³.

q: Which group directs an incoming electrophile mainly to the ortho and para positions of a benzene ring?
x: –OH has a lone pair on the oxygen next to the ring and donates electron density to the ortho and para positions. –CHO, –COOH and –SO₃H withdraw electrons and are meta directors.

q: Nitrobenzene undergoes electrophilic substitution much more slowly than benzene. The reason is that the –NO₂ group:
o: Donates electron density to the ring through a lone pair
Is so large that it blocks every position of the ring
Withdraws electron density from the ring, making it less attractive to electrophiles
Reacts with the electrophile before the ring can
x: –NO₂ pulls electrons out of the ring by both induction and resonance, lowering the electron density most at ortho and para, so the ring is deactivated and attack goes slowly to meta. Lone-pair donation describes activating groups such as –OH.

q: Benzoic acid, C₆H₅COOH, is brominated with Br₂ and FeBr₃. The main product is:
x: –COOH withdraws electrons and is a meta director, so Br goes to position 3. Treating –COOH like –OH gives the ortho/para products; tribromination happens only with strongly activated rings such as phenol.

q: Chlorobenzene reacts more slowly than benzene with electrophiles, yet substitution goes mainly to the ortho and para positions. This is because chlorine:
o: Donates electrons by both induction and resonance
Withdraws electrons by both induction and resonance
Has no effect on the ring's electron density
Withdraws electrons by its inductive effect but donates lone-pair electrons by resonance to the ortho and para positions
x: Chlorine's high electronegativity (−I) lowers the electron density of the whole ring, so it is deactivating. Its lone pairs (+M) put some electron density back at ortho and para, so those positions are attacked. A purely withdrawing group would direct meta.

q: Which compound gives only one mononitro product with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄?
x: In 1,4-dimethylbenzene all four ring hydrogens are equivalent, so only one product forms. 1,2-Dimethylbenzene has two kinds of ring H (positions 3 and 4), 1,3-dimethylbenzene three (2, 4 and 5), and methylbenzene three (ortho, meta, para).

q: 1,3-Dimethylbenzene is heated with excess hot alkaline KMnO₄ and the mixture is then acidified. The organic product is:
x: KMnO₄ oxidises every alkyl side chain on a benzene ring to –COOH while leaving the ring intact; with excess oxidant both methyl groups are oxidised. 3-Methylbenzoic acid assumes only one side chain reacts.

q: 4-Methylbenzoic acid, CH₃C₆H₄COOH (–CH₃ and –COOH para to each other), is nitrated with concentrated HNO₃ and H₂SO₄. The main product is:
o: An equal mixture of 4-methyl-2-nitrobenzoic acid and 4-methyl-3-nitrobenzoic acid
x: –CH₃ (at C4) directs ortho to itself, to C3 and C5; –COOH (at C1) directs meta, also to C3 and C5. Both groups agree, so the nitro group goes to C3. Position 2 is ortho to –COOH and meta to –CH₃, favoured by neither group; the side chain is not nitrated under these conditions.
